name: stub
intent: Replace a collaborator with a test-specific stand-in that returns canned answers, so the component under test can be driven down paths - success, empty, error, timeout - that the real collaborator cannot be made to produce on demand.
problem: The component under test receives indirect inputs through a collaborator, and the branch that must be exercised is selected by what that collaborator returns. The real collaborator will not produce the needed value on request: it is slow, remote, licensed, non-deterministic, or simply never returns the rare case - the empty result, the declined payment, the timeout - that the test exists for. Without a controllable replacement the test either cannot reach the path at all or has to provoke it through the production system, which is exactly what unit testing was supposed to avoid.
context: Unit and component tests of a component whose collaborators are already, or can cheaply become, abstractions: the values and exceptions a collaborator returns are inputs to the component under test, and the test asserts what the component does with them rather than how the collaboration happened. Typical where the collaborator is remote or stateful (HTTP client, database, queue, clock, payment gateway) or where the branch under test is an edge case - empty page, declined payment, expired token, feature off. The pattern assumes a substitutable seam: a constructor parameter, an injected interface, a factory, a lookup, or a patchable module.
benefits: Indirect inputs become ordinary test data: any branch of the component under test - success, empty, error, boundary - is reachable deterministically, without a fixture hunt through the real system.
The real collaborator is not needed, so the test is fast, repeatable and runnable anywhere: no network, database, licence, clock or seed data.
Isolation of the decision under test: the assertion is about what the component did with the answer, so the test survives refactorings of the collaborator and of its transport.
Non-determinism leaves the picture: the same canned answer every run removes flakiness caused by latency, clock, ordering or drifting data.
Contract-first development: the caller can be built and verified against the agreed response while the real adapter is still being written.
The programmed answers document the collaborator's contract in one visible place, which makes the assumed responses reviewable instead of implicit in the production call.
tradeoffs: The canned answers are an assumption about a contract that no test in the suite verifies: when the collaborator renames a method, changes an error type or adds an invariant, the stubbed test stays green, so every stubbed contract needs at least one test against the real implementation or a fake.

Stubbing needs a substitutable seam, so the pattern pushes interface extraction, dependency injection or module patching into production code; where legacy code offers none, the component under test must be edited before a single test can use a stub.

A stub cannot fail: it returns whatever the test programmed, so a passing test proves nothing about the real collaboration, and canned values that encode states production never reaches are a classic source of false confidence.

Because the stub never blocks, retries or times out, the component's timing, back-pressure and failure-handling paths are structurally unreachable through it; those need fakes, contract tests or integration tests.

Hand-written stubs duplicate setup across tests and drift into low-fidelity fakes once they must answer differently per test - Meszaros' Test Code Duplication and Obscure Test, solved only by factoring a Configurable Test Double or a fixture.

participants.responsibility: The component whose behaviour is the subject of the test; it consumes the collaborator's answers as indirect inputs and is unaware that it is talking to a stand-in.
Test-specific replacement for the collaborator, implementing its interface (or the part the SUT uses); it answers with the programmed values or exceptions and carries no expectations of its own.

The canned indirect inputs - a return value, a raised exception, or a sequence for consecutive calls - chosen to put the SUT on the path under test; Meszaros' Responder (valid or invalid returns) and Saboteur (errors) are the two flavours.
The abstraction the SUT already uses for the real collaborator; it is the contract the stub must satisfy and the reason a substitutable seam exists at all.
Configures the answers, installs the stub through the seam before the SUT is exercised, invokes the SUT and asserts the SUT's own results - never the stub's state.

use_cases: Exercising a rare branch of the component: an empty result set, a declined payment, a 429 from a gateway, a missing feature flag.
Testing error handling: programme the stub to raise the exception the real service would raise - timeout, connection reset, malformed payload - and assert that the SUT surfaces or recovers from it.
Unit-testing a component against a collaborator that is slow, paid, unavailable in CI or still being implemented; the stub encodes the agreed response while the real adapter is built.
Removing non-determinism from a path the real collaborator decides by clock, randomness or remote state (token expired, cache cold, retry budget exhausted), so one outcome can be asserted exactly.
View and presentation tests: a fixed dataset from the stub, so the assertion is about the rendering or the decision logic and nothing else.
Boundary values on contract edges - zero, maximum, empty string, unicode payloads - that the real system cannot be asked to return on demand.

Mockito (Java): when(warehouse.hasInventory(...)).thenReturn(false) programmes the declined-branch answer and thenThrow(SocketTimeoutException.class) injects the failure, and consecutive-value stubbing (thenReturn(v1, v2)) drives retry-then-succeed paths that the real warehouse would never produce on request.

Python unittest.mock (standard library): Mock(return_value=...) fixes the canned answer while side_effect set to an exception or an iterable raises or sequences answers per call - the library ships Responder and Saboteur behaviour as first-class configuration.

Moq (.NET): mock.Setup(x => x.HasInventory(...)).Returns(false) and .Throws<InvalidOperationException>() are the canned-answer primitives, so a C# test reaches the empty-inventory and fault branches of Order.Fill without touching a database.
avoid_when: The real collaborator is cheap and deterministic (a value object, a pure function, an in-memory collection): construct the real thing and delete the stub.
Behaviour depends on state built up over several calls (write-then-read, generated identifiers, sequences): use a Fake - an in-memory implementation - rather than programming every answer.
The interaction itself is the requirement (order, cardinality, arguments): use a Spy or a Mock, which record and verify; a stub is defined by what it returns.
No substitutable seam exists and the collaborator is final, sealed or static: introduce the seam or use a Test-Specific Subclass instead of reaching into internals.
The question is whether the real integration works: answer it with a contract test or a narrow integration test; a suite of stubs cannot.
The collaborator's behaviour is itself the thing worth testing (a parser, an algorithm, a state machine): test it directly; stubbing it away tests nothing.
anti_patterns: Green by construction: programming answers the real collaborator would never return and treating the passing test as evidence about production.
Asserting on the stub - its programmed value or its recorded calls - which is a spy/mock assertion smuggled into a stub and makes the test a tautology.
A hand-written stub class that grows one branch per test until it is an unfinished fake, with a fake's maintenance cost and none of its fidelity.
Deep stubbing: replacing an entire object graph with programmed stand-ins so that no production collaboration is exercised at all.
Patching the collaborator where the SUT does not look it up (wrong module or namespace), so the stub is never called and the test passes for the wrong reason.
Forgetting to reset or recreate the stub between tests, so one test's programmed answers leak into the next and produce order-dependent failures.
design_principles: Programme exactly the indirect inputs the branch consumes; every extra canned answer is an unverified assumption about the collaborator.
Depend on an abstraction before substituting it (dependency inversion): the stub must implement a contract the SUT already uses, not one invented for the test.
Separate control from observation: a stub answers; recording and verification are the Spy's and the Mock's job.
Substitute at the boundary the SUT already talks to, never inside the SUT's own logic.
Treat the stub as a hypothesis: validate every stubbed contract with at least one test against the real collaborator or a fake (contract test).
best_practices: Configure the answers before the stub is handed to the SUT; in most frameworks configuration after installation or after a call has no effect on calls already made.
Create a fresh stub (or reset it) per test so no programmed answer or recorded call leaks between tests.
Name the stub after the collaborator and the scenario (EmptyWarehouseStub, DeclinedPaymentStub) so a failure reads as the requirement it violates.

Prefer the framework's smallest canned-answer primitive (return_value, thenReturn, Returns, every { } returns, and_return, ON_CALL) over a hand-written class until the double genuinely needs real behaviour.
Keep at least one test per stubbed contract against the real implementation or a fake; the stub alone is an unchecked assumption.
When several tests need the same collaborator with different answers, promote the stub to a configurable test double or a fixture instead of copying the setup.
Assert the SUT's outcome, never the stub's state; if the test needs what the stub recorded, switch deliberately to a spy or a mock.
sources: Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code, Chapter 23 'Test Double Patterns' - Test Stub (p. 529), Addison-Wesley 2007.
